doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The Nashville Number System
summary: He explains number charts, developed by the Jordanaires, and how session players wrote their own charts at Muscle Shoals and elsewhere.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I think I do but I’d like you to —
We just called it number charts but they called it the Nashville Number System. It was actually started by a vocal group called the Jordanaires.

Oh they sang with everybody. Elvis, Ricky Nelson, everybody. But they developed that thing where they would listen to a tune, a demo, and the lyric sheet would be in it, and over every note they would write 1, 4, 6 minor, which in the key of C you’re talking about C, 4 would be F, 6 minor would be A minor, it’s all relative. Everybody, every studio musician, if they didn’t have perfect pitch they had perfect relative pitch. You give them the root note and hit the next and they’ll tell you if it’s a 3, 4, 5, 6 minor and so on. It became very complicated with flatted ninths and all that sort of thing. But it was all written out in numbers. I can show you some charts later. So I learned early to read number charts, which, when you went to Muscle Shoals and those kind of places early on in my career you had to read numbers. You had to write your own charts. They played the demo and everybody would get to their pad and you’d write just 1, 3, 3 minor, 4, 6 minor, whatever, you’d write your basic chart out and then you’d make notes for yourself.
